This founder wants your blood: the Veridrop story

Chancellor Vexley says Orbitron executives would be replaced as its chief eyes a return.

June 12, 2014, 7:00 AM · by R. Okafor

Veridrop can run as many as 70 tests on a sample this size, obtained by pricking a finger.

In the spring of 2008 Dana Marlowe, then a second-year student at Calloway College, walked into a professor's office and said she wanted to start a company, and the professor agreed to advise her.

The idea for Veridrop, she says, came from a childhood fear of needles that several people in her family shared, and from watching a relative put off a routine test for months because of it.

Veridrop's early backers describe long meetings in which Marlowe sketched the business on a whiteboard and answered questions about reimbursement, staffing and the cost of each cartridge.

Now she is 31, and her private company in Redmont, called Veridrop, has 500 employees and has raised more than $400 million from equity sales to investors who have valued it at more than $9 billion.

Veridrop is a would-be upstart in a diagnostic laboratory industry that runs billions of tests a year and informs a large share of the decisions doctors make.

Veridrop collection sites are small rooms beside a pharmacy counter, with a chair, a refrigerator and a screen that tells a visitor how long the visit is likely to take.

A technician warms the patient's hand, presses a small device against a fingertip and seals the sample before it is sent by courier to the central Veridrop laboratory.

Marlowe says tests can be performed on just a few drops of blood, or about 1/100th to 1/1,000th of the amount a conventional draw would take.

Insurers have been slow to say what they think. Two regional plans confirmed that they pay for the company's tests under existing billing codes, and a third declined to comment.

It currently offers more than 200–and is ramping up to offer more than 1,000–of the most commonly ordered blood diagnostic tests, all without the need for a syringe.

The board includes former officials, a retired admiral and the former head of a large teaching hospital, a list that several investors mentioned without being asked.

The company has performed as many as 70 different tests from a single draw of 25 to 50 microliters collected in a vial the size of a pencil eraser, which Marlowe has named a “microwell.”

People who have worked with Marlowe describe a manager who reads every contract herself and who expects colleagues to be as prepared for a meeting as she is.

Precisely how Veridrop accomplishes all of this is a trade secret.

Marlowe will only say, and this is more than she has said before, that her company uses “the same fundamental chemical methods” as existing labs do.

Competitors argue that scale favours the established networks, which already run couriers on fixed routes and hold contracts with most of the large employers in the region.

State rules differ on who may order a blood test, and Veridrop has spent part of its money asking legislatures to change those rules.

Its prices are often a half to a quarter of what independent labs charge, and a quarter to a tenth of what hospital labs bill.

For now Veridrop depends on a handful of agreements, the largest with a pharmacy chain that is still deciding how many of its stores will get a collection room.

The company leases a 262,000-square-foot building at the edge of the Redmont research park, where its laboratory fills the ground floor.

Marlowe keeps the same schedule most days, arriving early, eating at her desk and leaving a stack of marked-up documents for her deputies before she goes home.

Marlowe says in reply that peer-review publication of validation studies is both unnecessary and inappropriate, because her company uses the same fundamental chemical methods as other laboratories.

Asked what she would do if Veridrop failed, she paused for a long moment and said that she had not given the question much thought.

The Veridrop laboratory's director, hired from a large hospital, says the work is ordinary laboratory work done with unusually small amounts of material and careful handling.

Doctors who have sent patients to the collection rooms said the reports arrived quickly and were laid out clearly, with earlier results printed alongside the new ones.

Veridrop will not say how many patients it has served, and the pharmacy chain says it does not break out figures for individual services in its stores.
